problem: Let \( \rho : S_n \rightarrow \text{GL}(n, \mathbb{C}) \) be the homomorphism mapping a permutation \( g \) to its permutation matrix. Define \( \chi(g) = \text{Trace}(\rho(g)) \). Compute the value of \( \langle \chi, \chi \rangle = \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{g \in S_n} \chi(g)^2 \). Is this value always 2 for any \( n \)?

answer_text:
Let \(\chi(g)\) be the trace of the permutation matrix of \(g\). This trace is exactly the number of fixed points of \(g\):

\[
\chi(g)=\#\{i\in\{1,\dots,n\}:g(i)=i\}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\chi(g)^2
\]

counts the number of ordered pairs \((i,j)\) such that both \(i\) and \(j\) are fixed by \(g\). Hence

\[
\sum_{g\in S_n}\chi(g)^2
=
\#\{(g,i,j): g(i)=i,\ g(j)=j\}.
\]

We split into two cases.

### Case 1: \(i=j\)

There are \(n\) choices for \(i\). For a fixed \(i\), a permutation \(g\in S_n\) fixes \(i\) in \((n-1)!\) ways. Thus this contributes

\[
n(n-1)! = n!.
\]

### Case 2: \(i\neq j\)

There are \(n(n-1)\) ordered pairs \((i,j)\) with \(i\neq j\). For each such pair, \(g\) must fix both \(i\) and \(j\), which can be done in \((n-2)!\) ways. Thus this contributes

\[
n(n-1)(n-2)! = n!
\]

for \(n\ge 2\). For \(n=1\), this case is empty.

Therefore, for \(n\ge 2\),

\[
\sum_{g\in S_n}\chi(g)^2 = n!+n! = 2n!.
\]

So

\[
\langle \chi,\chi\rangle
=
\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{g\in S_n}\chi(g)^2
=
2.
\]

For \(n=1\), there is only the identity permutation, \(\chi(\mathrm{id})=1\), so

\[
\langle \chi,\chi\rangle = 1.
\]

Thus the value is

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
1, & n=1,\\[4pt]
2, & n\ge 2.
\end{cases}
}
\]

So it is not always \(2\) for every positive \(n\); it is \(2\) for all \(n\ge 2\).
